papers.title: Audio Jailbreaks in Large Audio-Language Models: Taxonomy, Attack-Defense Analysis, and Cost-Aware Evaluation
papers.abstract: Large Audio Language Models (LALMs) expand jailbreak risks from token-level prompting to the full speech perception-to-reasoning pipeline, where unsafe behavior can be induced through semantics, acoustic style, signal artifacts, or internal representations. Existing work studies these risks under heterogeneous threat models and evaluation protocols, making it difficult to compare attack practicality or defense utility. This paper provides a unified taxonomy and a controlled empirical evaluation of LALM jailbreak attacks and defenses. We organize prior work into semantic, acoustic, signal, and embedding-layer attacks; guard-based, training-free, and training-based defenses; and cross-modal, audio-native, and interactive benchmarks. We then evaluate representative attacks and defenses across ten open-source LALMs, measuring not only attack success rate but also benign refusal and latency. Our results show that Acoustic Best-of-N reveals strong worst-case audio-space vulnerabilities, Narrative Framing is an effective low-latency semantic threat, and current defenses trade robustness against benign usability. These findings support cost- and utility-aware evaluation as a necessary complement to success-rate-only LALM safety benchmarks.
papers.what: This paper provides a unified taxonomy and empirical evaluation of jailbreak attacks and defenses in large audio-language models (LALMs). It categorizes attacks and defenses, evaluates them across multiple LALMs, and introduces cost- and utility-aware evaluation metrics.
papers.novel: The paper introduces a unified taxonomy for LALM jailbreaks and defenses, and evaluates them using a comprehensive set of benchmarks, highlighting trade-offs between robustness and benign usability.
papers.method: The study organizes attacks and defenses into semantic, acoustic, signal, and embedding-layer categories, and evaluates them using cross-modal, audio-native, and interactive benchmarks.
papers.validation: The evaluation is conducted across ten open-source LALMs, measuring attack success rates, benign refusal rates, and latency to assess the practicality and utility of defenses.
papers.discussion: The findings reveal vulnerabilities in LALMs and highlight the need for balancing robustness and usability in defense mechanisms. Future work could explore more effective defenses and refine evaluation protocols.

papers.title: VoiceGiraffe: A Benchmark for Extreme Long-Context Audio-Language Understanding
papers.abstract: While large audio language models (LALMs) have achieved remarkable progress in audio processing at the second- or minute-level scale, understanding hour-level audio remains a fundamental bottleneck. Existing benchmarks predominantly rely on short clips or artificially concatenated segments, failing to faithfully assess LALM capacity for long-range information comprehension in real-world scenarios such as podcasts and lengthy speeches. To address this gap, we introduce VoiceGiraffe, a novel benchmark designed to rigorously evaluate LALMs across diverse real-world scenarios, modalities, and languages under long-context settings. It comprises 1500 curated triplets structured into a dual-level taxonomy of single-hop perception and multi-hop reasoning. We evaluate a broad suite of open-source and proprietary LALMs against human performance. Results underscore three fundamental findings. First, VoiceGiraffe remains highly challenging and far from saturation. Second, we show that no single inference paradigm universally dominates. The E2E inference benefits models with native long-context audio understanding, cascaded caption aggregation stabilizes small models overwhelmed by hour-scale audio, and reasoning-enhanced cascading with external LLM helps weaker models but can bottleneck stronger proprietary systems. Third, we reveal long-range memory persistence as a key bottleneck. LALMs are better at answering questions that require connecting salient causal cues than those requiring sustained tracking of sparse events across long audio, whereas humans show the opposite pattern. These findings position VoiceGiraffe as a challenging and diagnostic testbed for long-form audio understanding, highlighting the need for LALMs with persistent memory and robust long-range aggregation.
papers.what: This paper introduces VoiceGiraffe, a benchmark for evaluating LALMs on long-context audio understanding across diverse real-world scenarios, modalities, and languages.
papers.novel: VoiceGiraffe addresses the lack of benchmarks for hour-level audio understanding by providing a dual-level taxonomy of single-hop perception and multi-hop reasoning tasks.
papers.method: The benchmark consists of 1,500 curated triplets and evaluates LALMs on their ability to handle long-range memory persistence and aggregation of information over extended audio contexts.
papers.validation: The benchmark is used to evaluate both open-source and proprietary LALMs, comparing their performance against human baselines and identifying key bottlenecks in long-context understanding.
papers.discussion: The study highlights the challenges of long-range memory persistence and aggregation in LALMs, suggesting the need for models with robust memory mechanisms and better reasoning capabilities.

papers.title: Do Audio LLMs Listen or Read? Analyzing and Mitigating Paralinguistic Failures with VoxParadox
papers.abstract: Audio large language models (Audio LLMs) demonstrate strong performance on speech understanding tasks, yet their ability to understand paralinguistic information remains limited. To systematically quantify this issue, we introduce VoxParadox, an adversarial benchmark with 2,000 verified examples, spanning 10 paralinguistic tasks, created with controlled speech synthesis to intentionally mismatch transcript claims and speaking style, enabling direct measurement of speech paralinguistic understanding. Evaluation of a diverse set of Audio LLMs reveals consistently low accuracy on acoustic ground truth and a strong tendency to follow language-implied (incorrect) answers. To understand the cause of this gap, we perform layer-wise probing and find that (i) paralinguistic cues can degrade in deeper encoder layers and at the encoder--LLM interface, and (ii) even when such cues are available in audio tokens, the language model frequently ignores them. To address these problems, we propose Prompt-Conditioned Layer Mixer (PCLM), which adaptively combines information from multiple audio layers based on the input prompt, and pair it with Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) to explicitly prefer acoustically supported options over language-implied alternatives. These methods substantially improve Audio LLM paralinguistic understanding, improving Audio Flamingo 3 from 17.40% to 65.20% on VoxParadox, and from 37.74% to 54.78% on MMSU paralinguistic subset. Our project page is available at https://voxparadox.github.io/.
papers.comment: Accepted as a conference paper at ICML 2026. Project page: https://voxparadox.github.io/
papers.what: This paper introduces VoxParadox, an adversarial benchmark for evaluating paralinguistic understanding in Audio LLMs, and proposes the Prompt-Conditioned Layer Mixer (PCLM) to address identified limitations.
papers.novel: The study systematically quantifies the limitations of Audio LLMs in understanding paralinguistic information and introduces PCLM and Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) to improve performance.
papers.method: PCLM adaptively combines information from multiple audio layers based on input prompts, while DPO explicitly prefers acoustically supported options over language-implied alternatives.
papers.validation: The methods are validated on VoxParadox and the MMSU paralinguistic subset, showing significant improvements in paralinguistic understanding for Audio Flamingo 3.
papers.discussion: The study identifies the degradation of paralinguistic cues in deeper layers and the tendency of language models to ignore these cues, suggesting further research into integrating paralinguistic information effectively.

papers.title: Why Can't They Remember? Uncovering Representation and Retrieval Bottlenecks in Multi-Turn Acoustic Memory
papers.abstract: Large audio language models (LALMs) process both speech and environmental acoustic cues, yet struggle to retain non-speech information across multi-turn interactions. The performance gap between semantic (speech) and acoustic (non-speech) understanding remains poorly understood, and the underlying mechanisms of representation and retrieval are still unclear. This work introduces EnvMem, a controlled multi-turn benchmark designed to study this gap and identify the root causes of failures at the representation (i.e., latent embeddings) and retrieval levels (i.e., attention allocation). We further conduct post-hoc interventions to probe representational structure and attention dynamics. Our results reveal representational trajectory drift as the key failure mode, while showing that attention allocation plays a limited role in explaining the observed degradation. Overall, we provide a systematic framework for analyzing and improving non-linguistic memory in long-context LALMs, shedding light on future data and training design for robust acoustic memory modeling.
papers.what: This paper introduces EnvMem, a benchmark for studying multi-turn acoustic memory in LALMs, focusing on the gap between semantic and acoustic understanding.
papers.novel: The study identifies representational trajectory drift as a key failure mode in non-linguistic memory and provides a systematic framework for analyzing these issues.
papers.method: EnvMem evaluates LALMs on multi-turn interactions, probing representation and retrieval mechanisms to identify and address memory-related bottlenecks.
papers.validation: The benchmark is used to analyze representation and attention dynamics in LALMs, revealing the root causes of performance degradation in acoustic memory tasks.
papers.discussion: The findings suggest that improving representational stability is crucial for robust acoustic memory modeling, with attention allocation playing a secondary role.

papers.title: Natural Yet Challenging to Detect: Robust In-the-Wild TTS through EMA and Dual-Scoring Prompt Selection -- Submission for WildSpoof 2026 TTS Track
papers.abstract: In this technical report, we describe our submission for the WildSpoof Challenge TTS Track: Text-to-Speech with In-the-Wild Data. We introduce F5-TTS-DPS, a model built upon the F5-TTS architecture. Our approach integrates Exponential Moving Average (EMA) into supervised fine-tuning to stabilize training and improve generalization. To enhance synthesis fidelity, we leverage large language models (LLMs) and large audio language models (LALMs) for dual-scoring prompt selection, filtering reference audio and text prompts to ensure quality while addressing alignment issues in noisy datasets.   Experimental evaluation demonstrates that F5-TTS-DPS achieves strong performance with UTMOS of 3.20 and speaker similarity of 0.51 on the development set. More importantly, our model achieves the best a-DCF scores of 0.1582, 0.5233, and 0.2562 across three advanced SASV systems among all submissions, indicating our synthesized speech is the most difficult to detect and exhibits the highest degree of naturalness and authenticity. Combined with competitive WER performance, these results validate the effectiveness of our approach in generating natural-sounding speech with strong spoofing capabilities.
papers.what: This paper describes F5-TTS-DPS, a text-to-speech system designed for robust synthesis using in-the-wild data, submitted to the WildSpoof Challenge 2026 TTS Track.
papers.novel: The integration of Exponential Moving Average (EMA) for stable training and the use of dual-scoring prompt selection to filter noisy datasets are key innovations.
papers.method: The model builds on the F5-TTS architecture, incorporating EMA for fine-tuning and leveraging large language models and audio language models for dual-scoring prompt selection.
papers.validation: The system was evaluated on the WildSpoof 2026 dataset, achieving competitive UTMOS, speaker similarity, and a-DCF scores, demonstrating its naturalness and spoofing capabilities.
papers.discussion: The approach focuses on spoofing robustness, but its general applicability to other TTS tasks or datasets may require further investigation.

papers.title: cSTMM: A Unified Complex Spherical Student's $t$ Mixture Model for Directional Statistics in Mask-Based Blind Speech Separation
papers.abstract: Mask-based blind speech separation (BSS) estimates source-wise time-frequency (TF) masks by clustering multichannel observations using spatial information. The directional statistical approach clusters normalized multichannel observations on the complex unit sphere, without explicitly extracting phase and level difference features based on the plane-wave or spherical-wave assumptions. However, prior studies have mostly compared a small number of separately defined directional statistical mixture models, whereas a broader distribution family would enable a more systematic study of how density profiles affect separation performance.   We propose the complex spherical Student's t mixture model (cSTMM), a directional mixture model that connects the complex angular central Gaussian mixture model (cACGMM), complex Bingham mixture model (cBMM), and complex Watson mixture model (cWMM) through the degrees-of-freedom parameter $ν$. We also derive a generalized minorization-maximization (MM) based procedure for parameter estimation. A no-restart evaluation on noise-free LibriSpeech mixtures reverberated with measured room impulse responses shows that a single development-selected value $ν^\ast=1$ achieved higher test-set mean signal-to-distortion ratio improvements (SDRi) than the cACGMM-equivalent setting $ν=M$ in all acoustic conditions, with an average condition-wise gain of 0.25dB. The experiments also numerically verify that the proposed formulation numerically recovers the cACGMM, cBMM, and cWMM cases.
papers.what: This paper introduces the complex spherical Student's t mixture model (cSTMM) for mask-based blind speech separation, which clusters normalized multichannel observations on the complex unit sphere.
papers.novel: The proposed cSTMM unifies and generalizes several existing directional statistical mixture models (cACGMM, cBMM, cWMM) through a degrees-of-freedom parameter, enabling a systematic study of density profiles for separation performance.
papers.method: The cSTMM uses a generalized minorization-maximization procedure for parameter estimation and leverages a single development-selected parameter value to achieve improved signal-to-distortion ratio improvements.
papers.validation: The method was validated on noise-free LibriSpeech mixtures reverberated with measured room impulse responses, showing consistent SDRi improvements over the cACGMM-equivalent setting.
papers.discussion: The approach is limited to noise-free conditions and may require further research to handle noisy or more complex real-world scenarios effectively.

papers.title: Score-Agnostic Structure Analysis in Large-Scale Performance Datasets
papers.abstract: In recent years, thanks to advances in automatic music transcription (AMT), several large-scale datasets of automatically transcribed piano solo music have been released. While these datasets undoubtedly offer extensive material for performance studies, they vary substantially in quality.   In the case of classical music, performances often differ not only in expressive aspects such as tempo, but also in their structural interpretation of the score (including repeat patterns and edition-specific variants). To meaningfully use large-scale transcribed datasets for performance research, transcriptions of the same piece must be grouped according to their underlying structural realisation to support valid comparison.   We address this by applying sequence-to-sequence alignment followed by hierarchical clustering: we create pairwise alignments for all pairs of transcriptions of a given piece, and use the alignment cost and (dis)similarity of performed sequence lengths to resolve structural mismatches as features for grouping. We propose this approach as a first step towards automatically evaluating large-scale transcribed datasets that lack ground-truth score and/or audio, shifting the evaluation criterion from truth-based accuracy to musical coherence and plausibility.   We demonstrate our score-agnostic approach on around 1,500 transcriptions of 88 compositions from a recently published large-scale transcribed piano performance dataset.
papers.comment: published at the Music Encoding Conference (MEC) 2026
papers.what: This paper proposes a score-agnostic method for analyzing structural variations in large-scale transcribed piano performance datasets, focusing on musical coherence rather than ground-truth accuracy.
papers.novel: The study shifts the evaluation criterion from truth-based accuracy to musical coherence, enabling meaningful comparisons of performances with structural mismatches.
papers.method: The method uses sequence-to-sequence alignment and hierarchical clustering to group transcriptions based on structural realization, leveraging alignment costs and sequence length similarities.
papers.validation: The approach is demonstrated on 1,500 transcriptions of 88 compositions from a large-scale piano performance dataset, showcasing its ability to identify structural mismatches.
papers.discussion: The method provides a new perspective for evaluating transcribed datasets but may require further refinement to handle more complex musical structures and diverse datasets.

papers.title: Rubato: Transcribing Piano Music with Timestamps
papers.abstract: We consider the conversion of musical recordings into human-readable sheet music annotated with timestamps. Such output lets a listener clearly visualize rubato (temporally expressive playing), a learner diagnose ensemble precision and timing choices against the written music, and a musicology scholar compare performance styles across recordings of the same work. We introduce (1) a prompt-conditioned encoder-decoder model, named Rubato, trained to output (2) a new textual representation for polyphonic music, named InterMo, which we designed for compatibility with sequence-to-sequence training. Our experiments demonstrate that Rubato produces timestamped piano sheet music from audio with higher notational accuracy than the best existing approaches, which are based on cascades. We find that even if the cascade is given ground-truth MIDI instead of audio, Rubato performs better, suggesting that the ceiling of existing approaches is primarily representational, not acoustic. Further, because Rubato is trained on several related tasks (with prompts), it competes with or outperforms the best single-task systems on related but simpler tasks like MIDI note grounding and beat/downbeat detection. A demo is available at https://nctamer.github.io/rubato-transcription .
papers.what: This paper presents Rubato, a prompt-conditioned encoder-decoder model for transcribing piano music into timestamped sheet music using a new textual representation called InterMo.
papers.novel: Rubato outperforms existing cascade-based approaches by addressing representational limitations and introducing a unified model trained on multiple related tasks.
papers.method: The model uses a sequence-to-sequence framework with prompt conditioning and the InterMo representation, designed for compatibility with polyphonic music transcription tasks.
papers.validation: Rubato was evaluated on piano transcription tasks, demonstrating higher notational accuracy and better performance on related tasks like beat detection compared to state-of-the-art methods.
papers.discussion: The method's reliance on task-specific prompts may limit generalizability to other instruments or musical styles without further adaptation.

papers.title: Music Transcription with (Almost) No Supervision
papers.abstract: Competitive music transcription models require large amounts of paired audio-score data, which is scarce due to collection costs, alignment difficulty, and copyright restrictions. Meanwhile, vast quantities of unpaired audio recordings and symbolic scores are freely available but have gone unused. We adopt a cycle-consistent translation framework in which a small amount of paired data acts as a minimal anchor, unlocking the full potential of the unpaired pool. We find that: unpaired data yields surprisingly large gains, especially under limited supervision; unpaired audio contributes more than unpaired scores; incorporating unlabeled audio from a new instrument during training improves transcription for that instrument without any paired supervision. Together, these results suggest that scaling unpaired data offers a practical path toward high-quality transcription for instruments where labeled data remains scarce.
datasets: Custom unpaired audio and symbolic scores
papers.what: This paper explores a cycle-consistent translation framework for music transcription with minimal supervision, leveraging unpaired audio and symbolic scores.
papers.novel: The approach demonstrates that unpaired data can significantly improve transcription performance, especially in low-supervision settings, and that unpaired audio contributes more than unpaired scores.
papers.method: The framework uses a small amount of paired data as an anchor to unlock the potential of unpaired data, with a focus on cycle-consistency to bridge the gap between audio and symbolic domains.
papers.validation: The method was validated on transcription tasks with limited paired data, showing significant performance improvements and generalization to new instruments using only unpaired audio.
papers.discussion: The reliance on unpaired data may limit performance in scenarios where such data is not available or is of low quality; further exploration of domain adaptation is needed.
